children.name: Menura
children.description: Lyrebirds — ancient Australian passerines renowned as the world's foremost avian mimics. The male's extraordinary tail, shaped like a Greek lyre when fanned, is the most elaborate of any bird. They can imitate any sound — from other birds' songs to chainsaws, camera shutters, and car alarms — with astonishing fidelity. Despite their superb mimicry, lyrebirds are rarely seen, spending most of their time scratching through forest leaf litter for invertebrates.

children.name: Menura novaehollandiae
children.description: The superb lyrebird (Menura novaehollandiae) is an Australian passerine songbird, one of two species from the family Menuridae, with the other being the much rarer Albert's lyrebird.

children.name: Menura alberti
children.description:
Albert's lyrebird (Menura alberti), sometimes known as the northern lyrebird, is a timid, pheasant-sized songbird which is endemic to subtropical rainforests of Australia, in a small area on the state border between New South Wales and Queensland. The rarer of the two species of lyrebirds, Albert's lyrebird is named after Prince Albert, the prince consort of Queen Victoria, queen of the United Kingdom. It lacks the elegant lyre-shaped tail feathers of the superb lyrebird and is found in a much more restricted range.
The total population of Albert's lyrebirds was estimated at only 3,500 breeding birds in 2000, with one of the smallest distributional ranges of any bird on the continent.
